q: How does a similarity s(A,B) differ from a distance d(A,B)?
a: Similarity is large when close; distance is small
w: They are identical, just with different names
Similarity can be any negative or positive number
Distance always lies in [0,1], like a probability
e: Similarity is large (usually 1) when objects are close and lies in [0,1]; distance is small (usually 0) when close and lies in [0,∞]. You can often convert with d = 1 − s, or d = √(s(A,A) + s(B,B) − 2s(A,B)).
The intersection is {0,2,5} (3 elements). The union has 8 elements.

q: The symmetric difference AΔB is:
a: Elements in A or B but not both
w: Elements in both A and B
Elements in A but not in B
Elements in neither A nor B
e: (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B): elements in A or B but not both. It appears in the generalized set similarity family S_{x,y,z,z′}.

q: Sørensen-Dice similarity equals:
e: The other options are Jaccard, Hamming, and Andberg similarity.

q: For which set similarities is 1 − S a metric AND amenable to LSH?
w: Only Sørensen-Dice and nothing else
All of them, including Sørensen-Dice
None of the standard set similarities
e: See Chierichetti & Kumar, SODA 2012.

q: A k-gram (k-shingle) is:
a: k consecutive words or characters as one unit
w: The k most common words in the document
A single word repeated k times in a row
A random sample of k words from the text
e: A group of k consecutive words (or characters) treated as one object. The set of 1-grams is exactly the bag-of-words model.

q: General rule for choosing k in k-grams:
a: Large enough that any one k-gram is rare
w: Always use k = 1, like bag of words
Use k equal to the document's length
Use the smallest k that is possible
e: Make k large enough that the probability of almost any k-gram is low, so a collision is meaningful. Emails: k = 2–3. Research articles: k = 3–4. With 27 characters and k = 5 there are ~14 million possible character grams.

q: Which modeling choice is typically different between bag-of-words and k-gramming?
w: Whether words are used at all
Whether any words are kept
Whether stop words are included
e: Bag of words typically counts replicas; k-gramming does not. Other choices: whitespace, capitalization, punctuation, characters vs. words, stop words.

q: A trick for stop words in shingling is:
a: 3-grams that must start with a stop word
w: Delete every word that appears twice
Keep only the stop words themselves
Set k to 0 so nothing is shingled
e: Use k = 3 grams where the first word must be a stop word (e.g., 'the pizza oven'). Stop words: a, you, for, the, to, and, that, it, is...

q: With 2-grams, D1 'I am Sam.' = {[I am],[am Sam]} and D2 'Sam I am.' = {[Sam I],[I am]}. JS(D1,D2) = ?
e: They share only [I am], and the union has 3 grams.

q: In CBOW for words, a word's vector representation is:
a: The average of its context-count vectors
w: The vector from its first occurrence only
A random vector assigned to each word
An encoding of the word's spelling
e: The average of the context-count vectors over all instances of that word. Distances can then use Jaccard on the sets, or cosine/Euclidean on the vectors. r = 5 has been suggested for large corpora.

q: A hash h is (γ, φ, α, β)-sensitive w.r.t. d if:
a: Close pairs collide with prob. > α; far pairs < β
w: Every pair of points always collides under h
Collision probability is uniform for all pairs
Close pairs never collide, and far pairs always do
e: We need α > β with γ < φ. Ideally α − β is large and φ − γ is small.

q: How does a locality-sensitive hash differ from the random hash functions in L2?
a: LSH makes close items more likely to collide
w: LSH is deterministic, random hashes aren't
LSH never produces any collisions at all
There is no difference between the two
e: LSH makes collisions MORE likely for close items; random hashes are uncorrelated. Think of a random grid over spatial data.

q: The key property of MinHash is:
w: Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = 1 − JS(A,B)
h(A) is always unique
e: So averaging collisions over t hash functions estimates the Jaccard similarity.

q: To compute MinHash h_j(S):
a: Take the minimum hash over the set's elements
w: Hash the whole set as a single long string
Take the maximum element in the set
Count how many elements are in the set
e: Initialize v_j = ∞; for each element i of S, keep the minimum of h′_j(i). Fast MinHash runs k hashes in one pass: |S|·k steps, independent of the universe size.

q: In the permutation proof, with x rows having 1 in both columns and y rows having 1 in exactly one, Pr[m(Sᵢ) = m(Sⱼ)] = ?
w: x / (x + y + z)
y / (x + y)
z / (x + y + z)
e: x / (x + y) = JS(Sᵢ, Sⱼ). The first non-empty row in the random permutation is type x with probability x/(x+y).

q: How many MinHash functions k give error ≤ ε with probability ≥ 1 − δ?
w: k = (1/ε) ln(n) for n elements
k = (n ln n) / ε for the set size n
k = √(2n) / δ for universe size n
e: From Chernoff-Hoeffding with Δᵢ = 1. Note it's independent of set size.

q: For ε = 0.05 and δ = 0.01, about how many MinHash functions are needed?
w: About 20
About 200
About 100,000

q: In the bears analogy, 'Papa bear' only checks pairs that collide in ALL hashes, and 'Mama bear' checks pairs colliding in ANY hash. What's the problem?
a: Papa checks almost nothing; Mama almost everything
w: Both strategies are perfect for any number of hashes
Papa checks every pair; Mama checks almost nothing
Mama never finds any collisions in the data
e: With many hashes, Papa checks almost nothing and Mama checks almost everything. 'Baby bear likes banding.'

q: With r bands of b hashes each and similarity s, the probability a pair becomes a candidate is:
w: f(s) = s^(r·b) for all r, b
f(s) = 1 − s^r, ignoring b
f(s) = (1 − s)^b, ignoring r
e: s^b = all hashes in a band collide. (1 − s^b)^r = no band fully collides.

q: The banding S-curve's steepest point (threshold τ) is roughly:
w: τ = r·b
τ = 1/2 always
τ = b/r
e: Without a budget limit, increasing r and b makes the S-curve sharper.

q: With r = 5 bands of b = 3 hashes, f(0.5) ≈ ?
LSH for Euclidean distance: project points onto a random unit vector u, then:
a: Bin the line into width-γ cells; the bin is the hash
w: Take the sign of the projection as a ±1 hash value
Take the minimum coordinate of the projected point
Sort all of the points by their projected value
e: Projection is contractive. It's (γ/2, 2γ, 1/2, 1/3)-sensitive.

q: Easiest way to generate a random unit vector in ℝᵈ:
w: Draw coordinates uniformly from [0,1]
Take a column of the identity matrix
Pick a random data point as the vector
e: Draw each coordinate as an independent 1-D Gaussian (e.g., via Box-Muller), then normalize. A uniform Gaussian has independent coordinates in any orthogonal basis.

q: Which distributions are 2-stable and 1-stable, respectively?
w: Cauchy and Gaussian
Uniform and Poisson
Exponential and Gaussian
e: Gaussian (2-stable) and Cauchy (1-stable). They give LSH for L2 and L1 norms. p-stable distributions exist for p ∈ (0, 2].

q: L1-normalizing a count vector puts it in the (m−1)-simplex Δ^(m−1). Unlike the sphere S^(m−1), the simplex:
a: Is convex, so line segments stay inside it
w: Has no corners or boundary points at all
Contains vectors with negative entries
Is curved, like the surface of a sphere
e: Is a linear (convex) space, so straight line segments stay inside it. It's the convex hull of the standard basis vectors e₁...e_m.

q: Total Variation distance between distributions a and b equals:
w: ‖a − b‖₂
Σ aⱼ ln(aⱼ/bⱼ)
max CDF difference
e: It inherits metric properties from L1 and is the most sensitive metric on distributions.

q: Hellinger distance can be interpreted as:
a: Square-root onto the sphere, then Euclidean distance
w: The extra bits to describe b given knowledge of a
The largest gap between the two distributions' CDFs
The cost of moving earth from one pile to the other
e: 'Lifting' distributions onto a wedge of the sphere (via square roots), then using Euclidean distance. d_H = (1/√2)·√Σ(√aⱼ − √bⱼ)². It's a metric on the simplex.

q: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between 1-D distributions is:
w: The average CDF difference
Σ µ(z) ln(µ(z)/ν(z))
The earth mover's distance
e: It's computed by sorting and scanning, and works over any totally ordered domain.

q: Why is Total Variation a poor choice for continuous data like rainfall?
a: It ignores how close nearby values are
w: It isn't actually a proper metric at all
It is much too slow to compute in practice
It needs labeled training data to be used
e: No two observations may match exactly (TV ≈ 1), and it ignores that 1.0012 is close to 1.0014. KS (in 1-D) and Wasserstein/MMD account for geometry.

q: Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) corresponds to which Wasserstein distance?
w: W₂
W∞
W₀
e: It's the minimum cost of moving 'piles of dirt' P into 'holes' Q. W₂ has nicer computational properties.

q: Generic exact computation of W₁/W₂ given all pairwise distances takes about:
w: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log n)
e: Sinkhorn (entropy-regularized, convex) gives an ε-approximation of W₂ in about O((1/ε) n² log n).

q: Kernel distance between points: d_K(p,q) = ?
w: K(p,p) + K(q,q) − K(p,q)²
1 − K(p,q)² / K(p,p)
e: It mirrors ‖p − q‖² = ⟨p,p⟩ + ⟨q,q⟩ − 2⟨p,q⟩. Its range is [0, √2].

q: Which listed kernel is NOT positive definite?
w: Gaussian
Laplace
General Gaussian on a metric space
e: All are in [0,1], but positive definiteness is what makes d_K a metric.

q: An advantage of MMD/kernel distance over Wasserstein:
a: No transport plan to solve, and robust to outliers
w: It always matches every point one-to-one
It never needs any all-pairs computation
It catches every mode better than Wasserstein
e: No optimal transport plan to solve, and it's resistant to outliers. W₂ is more refined: it matches every point, gives better alignment, and doesn't miss modes.

q: Replacing every dot product ⟨p,q⟩ in an L2 formulation with K(p,q) is called:
w: Banding
Min-hashing
The Box-Muller transform
e: In the RKHS, d_K(P,Q) = ‖KDE_P − KDE_Q‖, hence the name 'maximum mean discrepancy'.
